title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
summary: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control.

title: Prediction of early Toxoplasma gondii infection during pregnancy combining host biomarkers and machine learning
summary: Toxoplasma gondii is a major cause of reproductive failure and severe gestational complications in both humans and small ruminants and early diagnosis is essential to prevent adverse outcomes. In sheep, congenital toxoplasmosis can trigger early fetal death (EFD) during the acute phase of the infection (days 7-14 post-infection) when conventional diagnosis methods are ineffective. Therefore, this study aimed to identify early infection biomarkers using a machine learning approach to support EFD diagnosis and providing a translational foundation for early diagnostic strategies in human toxoplasmosis. For that, 27 serum biomarkers (cytokines, acute-phase proteins, oxidative stress and hemostatic parameters) were evaluated during the early stage of infection in 22 pregnant sheep experimentally challenged with T. gondii and 6 uninfected controls. To assess diagnostic specificity, models were tested using sera from animals experimentally infected with other abortifacient agents (Neospora caninum and Chlamydia abortus) and validated with samples from 19 natural abortion outbreaks. A four-biomarkers panel, encompassing CXCL9, CXCL10, IFN-{gamma}, and serum amyloid A, achieved over 74% accuracy in the specific detection of early T. gondii infection and 100% of sensitivity when studying natural infection cases. This approach might support the development of rapid diagnostic strategies, improving early intervention and disease management in livestock production systems. Its translation to human medicine could also aid in addressing current diagnostic gaps and facilitate timely interventions to prevent congenital toxoplasmosis and pregnancy loss in women.

title: Dissociable Oscillatory Alpha and Aperiodic Neural Dynamics Underlie Atypical Attentional Control in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
summary: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often have difficulty maintaining goal-directed attention when task-relevant and task-irrelevant information compete for processing resources. The present study investigated whether this difficulty reflects distinct abnormalities in demand-related attentional regulation and distractor-related neural responses. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) signals from 45 children with ADHD and 45 typically developing (TD) children while they performed a visual detection task under low and high visual demands, with simultaneous task-irrelevant standard and deviant sounds. EEG power spectra were parameterized to separate oscillatory alpha activity from aperiodic activity, as putative indices of attentional regulation and cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, respectively. TD children showed adaptive demand-related alpha modulation, whereas children with ADHD showed an atypical alpha response pattern, including reduced frontal modulation and atypical posterior alpha enhancement; this demand-related group difference was observed in oscillatory alpha activity but not in aperiodic activity. In contrast, ADHD-related abnormalities in responses to auditory distractors were more clearly reflected in the aperiodic slope. Children with ADHD showed atypical distractor-related aperiodic modulation, suggesting reduced stability of neural background activity, potentially reflecting disrupted cortical E/I balance when irrelevant sounds had to be ignored. Furthermore, multivariate machine learning classification demonstrated that relying on these sensitive neural signatures yielded robust discrimination between children with ADHD and TD controls, with significant predictive performance emerging shortly after stimulus onset and sustaining throughout information processing. These findings suggest that oscillatory alpha activity and aperiodic neural dynamics show differential sensitivity to distinct attentional abnormalities in ADHD, with alpha oscillations primarily reflecting demand-related regulatory deficits and aperiodic activity primarily reflecting distractor-related neural instability.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer's Disease
summary: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods: We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5*5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results: Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 +- 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 +- 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 +- 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion: These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

title: Role of Very Long-Chain Fatty Acyl-Ceramides in Endocytic Uptake
summary: Specialized endoplasmic reticulum (ER) subdomains termed ER sterol exit sites (ERSES), transiently contact endocytic sites to locally supply sterols, which in turn initiate actin polymerization and drive membrane invagination. Osh2, an oxysterol-binding protein (OSBP)-related protein (ORP), mediates the non-vesicular sterol transfer at ER-endocytic contact sites (ER-ECS). In search for additional ERSES components, we identified Fat1, a fatty acid (FA) transporter and acyl-CoA synthetase with specificity for very long-chain (VLC) FAs (C20-C26). Analysis of VLC-FA anabolic and catabolic pathways revealed a specific requirement for VLC fatty acyl-ceramides (VLCA-Cers) in the constriction of endocytic invaginations. Strikingly, the Cer synthase physically interacted with the endocytic machinery, pointing to a direct role of VLCFA-Cers in membrane remodelling. Consistent with this view, molecular dynamics and live-cell imaging of a Cer probe indicated that the ORPs Osh1 and Osh3 contribute to Cer export from at ER-ECS and and that their depletion recapitulates the endocytic defects observed in the absence of VLCFA-Cer. Our findings establish that local transport of VLCA-Cers is required for endocytic budding and reveal ERSES as hubs where Cer and sterol biosynthesis and transport converge

title: Histone H3 cysteines as redox switches in the nucleosome: molecular modeling of S-sulfenylation and its structural consequences
summary: Oxidation of buried histone cysteines links cellular redox signaling to chromatin regulation. Histone H3 carries two such residues: C96, unique to the H3.1 variant, and C110, shared by most H3 variants. Oxidation of H3.1 C96 by H2O2 drives histone variant exchange and chromatin opening in cancer cells, and C110 undergoes S-glutathionylation, yet both thiols are shielded from the solvent. How they are oxidized and what the modification does to the nucleosome structure remain unknown. Combining all-atom molecular dynamics, QM/MM and free energy calculations, we reveal S-sulfenylation mechanisms at both cysteines within the nucleosome core particle, from oxidant access to its structural consequences. Reaching either cysteine costs ~12 kcal/mol, paid mostly for the desolvation of H2O2 independently of the entry route. The reaction is then enabled in the hydrophobic environment by the presence of a single neighboring base. Such a residue is already in place at C110 (H3D123), but must first reorganize at C96 (H3E97), with barriers of ~18 kcal/mol at both sites. Once formed, the modification acts well beyond its site. C96 S-sulfenylation acts on DNA-histone interfaces, on elements recognized by chromatin remodelers and chaperones (H2AE91 at the acidic patch, H2A C-term release), and on the H4K91-H2B'D68 salt bridge bridging the two halves of the nucleosome. C110 oxidation mainly favors unwrapping and DNA destabilization at the dyad. These results provide a structural framework for understanding histone-mediated redox signaling and its implication in chromatin remodeling.

title: The Molecular Interplay of Tau and Motor Proteins on Microtubules
summary: Tau is a microtubule (MT)-associated protein essential for neuronal cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport, yet how tau physically regulates motor proteins remains elusive. Here, we integrate single-molecule imaging, cryo-electron microscopy, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying tau-mediated inhibition of kinesin-1 and cytoplasmic dynein motility. We show that tau suppresses MT landing and triggers frequent pausing and premature detachment when motors encounter tau-enriched patches. Unexpectedly, tau impairs each motor using different mechanisms. Tau and kinesin-1 compete for the same surface on tubulin, precluding simultaneous binding to the same MT site. On the other hand, while dynein and tau can co-occupy the same tubulin, tau inhibits the transition of dynein into its high-affinity MT-binding state. Thus, tau can act as a physical or a conformational roadblock in a concentration-dependent manner, exerting distinct structural constraints on kinesin and dynein transport. These findings establish a structural framework for tau-mediated regulation of axonal transport.

title: Contributions of Site Heterogeneity in Multi-site Brain-Phenotype Predictions
summary: Machine learning studies of brain-phenotype associations typically summarize accuracy with a single Pearson correlation, yet in harmonized multi-site data this metric is shaped by training-set size, feature and outcome variability, and true effect heterogeneity. We analyzed structural MRI data from the Reproducible Brain Charts consortium. After preprocessing and quality control, 3486 participants from 9 sites were retained. Three training set compositions were used to understand contributions of site heterogeneity after harmonization: within-site (Local), size-downsampled multi-site (Multi-Down), and full multi-site (Multi-Full). Another site-agnostic strategy (Overall) pooled all sites into a single dataset. All strategies included the target site in the training and testing samples. These analyses separate the contribution of the site effect from that of sample size. Between-site heterogeneity was extensive (age I^2 {approx} 95%). The overall correlation of age prediction (r = 0.73) exceeded the within-site meta-analytic estimate (Multi-Full r = 0.63). The improvement of correlation in the pooled dataset was driven by a mechanical inflation from the larger outcome variance. At matched sample size, within-site training outperformed harmonized multi-site training. Increasing the multi-site training sample size did not yield a significant advantage over within-site training. The apparent advantage of cross-dataset training thus appears to reflect training-set size rather than a benefit of multi-site composition per se. The same pattern generally held for the weaker brain-p-factor signals. Together, these results indicate that between-site heterogeneity in machine learning brain-phenotype prediction persists after harmonization. We recommend reporting site-level prediction accuracy and feature dispersion and standard deviation of the outcome variable alongside any pooled estimate to improve inter-site and inter-study comparison of machine learning prediction accuracy.

title: How the Azadithiolate Ligand Impacts O2-Stability of Group B -Hydrogenase ToHydA
summary: [FeFe]-hydrogenases are metalloenzymes that catalyze the reversible oxidation and production of H2, making them potential candidates for sustainable energy solutions. However, their practical application is restricted by their extreme O2 sensitivity, which leads to irreversible active site degradation. A newly characterized Group B hydrogenase, ToHydA from Thermosediminibacter oceani, has exhibited exceptional O2-stability even after long-term exposure to air. In ToHydA, the highly conserved proton-transporting cysteine (C212) safeguards the H-cluster from O2-induced degradation by formation of the Hinact state. In this study, we investigate the effects of replacing the azadithiolate (ADT) ligand of [2Fe]H with propanedithiolate (PDT), revealing that this substitution prevents the formation of the Hinact and Htrans states observed in ToHydA WT (bearing the ADT ligand). By combining ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we show that a favorable interaction between the nitrogen bridgehead of the ADT ligand and the C212 sidechain is crucial for stabilizing these states. The absence of this interaction in ToHydAPDT (bearing the PDT ligand) prevents the C212 sidechain from approaching the Fed center of [2Fe]H, thereby reducing Hinact accumulation. Moreover, as-isolated ToHydAPDT predominantly exhibits the Hhyd state, which is unusual for [FeFe]-hydrogenases with bound PDT ligand. These findings demonstrate how ligand substitution at the [2Fe]H site of ToHydA affects the structural dynamics, offering detailed molecular insights into the ligand-dependent modulation of [FeFe]-hydrogenases.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Structural Prioritization of Sulforaphane Targets in Neurodegeneration: A Multi-Dataset In Silico Study
summary: Sulforaphane (SFN), a natural isothiocyanate from cruciferous vegetables, exerts neuroprotective effects through mechanisms extending beyond canonical Nrf2/ARE activation. Here, we developed a multi-dataset computational framework integrating transcriptomic analysis, multi-criteria target prioritization, and structural docking evaluation. R- and S-SFN were docked against 693 prioritized targets using AutoDock Vina, followed by cross-validation, brain expression profiling, and molecular dynamics simulations. Four genes (IGSF9, KCNQ5, KCTD12, and NFIX) were dysregulated across all four datasets. Among 693 targets, 88 showed favorable predicted docking scores (deltaG less than or equal to -4.0 kcal/mol), with 65 (73.9%) exhibiting expression in at least one GTEx brain region. Independent cross-validation showed significant enrichment of prioritized targets in an SFN-responsive Alzheimer disease transcriptomic dataset (OR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.08-1.89, p = 0.0104). Complementary disease gene set enrichment confirmed that 33% of strong hits (29/88) overlap established neurodegeneration gene sets across AD, PD, and ALS - including ACHE, target of FDA-approved anti-AD drugs - with highly significant enrichment across all three disease categories (OR range: 67-127, all p less than 0.001). R-SFN showed a modest but statistically detectable preference over S-SFN across the 88 strong hits (Wilcoxon p = 0.0081; paired t-test p = 0.0047). TMEM45A, GRIK2, and FABP3 emerged as putative neurodegeneration-relevant targets. Molecular dynamics simulations supported the structural stability of R-SFN poses for TMEM45A, GRIK2, and FABP3, while MM-GBSA estimated favorable binding energies for GRIK2 (deltaG_bind = -19.78 kcal/mol) and FABP3 (deltaG_bind = -14.49 kcal/mol). These findings generate testable hypotheses regarding previously underexplored molecular targets that may contribute to the neuroprotective actions of SFN.

title: A timeline for evolution of metabolism in early microbes
summary: The metabolism of early microbes shaped our planet's chemistry and enabled more life to evolve. However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4 billion years ago (Ga) with fermentation and sulfur compound respiration. A second wave began ~3.2 Ga with aerobic respiration and growth, while a third began ~1.4 Ga with further specialization. We compared these predictions with independent dates from the geochemical record, and agreement with conservative dates was good (CCC = 0.81 to 0.89). Several forms of metabolism are invisible in the geochemical record, and our approach dates these forms, too. Our results reconcile different lines of evidence for microbial evolution and provide a fuller picture of early Earth.

title: Structural basis for inefficient G protein coupling by Frizzled receptors
summary: Frizzleds (FZDs) are class F G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that primarily signal through Dishevelled (DVL) to initiate Wnt signalling, with evidence for context-specific coupling to heterotrimeric G proteins. Every FZD-G protein structure to date has been determined without an agonist, implying that agonist binding is not required for stable complex formation in vitro and directly contradicting the difficulty of demonstrating G protein coupling in cells. All these structures contain unassigned density between the receptor and the heterotrimeric G protein. From structures generated by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) of FZD7-Gs and FZD5-Gq, we identify this density as the detergent lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG), which bridges the receptor and G protein to stabilise a weak, shallow interface. Absence of LMNG - in biochemical preparations and molecular dynamics simulations - destabilises the complex, showing that constitutive FZD-G protein engagement is intrinsically weak. The weak G protein coupling is governed by a conserved intracellular interface that when mutated differentially influences DVL and G protein signalling. Our findings show that LMNG has masked the instability of purified FZD-G protein complexes and provide the structural basis of FZDs as inherently weak G protein activators that are predisposed to DVL signalling.

title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
summary: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Together, these complementary analyses provide supporting evidence for the clinical relevance and biological consistency of MODAE+ predictions, suggesting their potential to identify drug-sensitive tumour subgroups and generate hypotheses about mechanisms of drug resistance.

title: The binding landscape of Ras/effector interactions provides insights on Ras switching and oncogenesis
summary: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) regulate essential cellular processes, yet the evolutionary principles that shape their specificity, adaptability, and dysregulation in disease remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the evolution of a signaling PPI between the small GTPase Ras and its effector Nore1A, a tumor suppressor involved in Ras-mediated signaling. Ras acts as a molecular switch, engaging effectors in its GTP-bound active state and releasing them after GTP hydrolysis, whereas oncogenic mutations such as G12D lock Ras in the active state, promoting aberrant signaling in cancer. Using yeast surface display, deep mutational scanning, and data normalization, we systematically mapped the Ras/Nore1A binding landscape under different physiological and oncogenic states. We generated and screened $\sim$33,000 Nore1A single and double mutants against RasWT and RasG12D in both GTP- and GDP-bound states. Our data revealed that most Nore1A mutations produce small-to-moderate decrease in Ras affinity, while a small number of substitutions enhance affinity. Unexpectedly, GTP hydrolysis causes minimal remodeling of the interaction landscape. Conversely, the oncogenic RasG12D mutation reshapes the binding landscape, revealing many Nore1A variants with enhanced and selective affinity for mutant Ras. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Nore1A-Ras variant complexes suggest that the non-optimality of the Nore1A/RasG12D binding landscape arises, in part, from the greater intrinsic flexibility of RasG12D and the pronounced reduction in flexibility induced by affinity-enhancing Nore1A mutations. These findings demonstrate that disease-associated mutations can create new evolutionary trajectories in signaling PPIs by changing interaction dynamics and provide a framework for engineering selective protein-based inhibitors targeting oncogenic Ras variants.

title: AnDi-J: diffusion analysis of single-particle tracking data in Fiji
summary: Characterizing how particles diffuse is key to understanding biology across scales, yet extracting the underlying physical properties typically requires specialized tools rarely accessible to biology labs. Here we introduce AnDi-J, a Fiji plugin combining classical estimators with state-of-the-art machine learning for single-trajectory analysis and segmentation, requiring minimal knowledge of stochastic processes. It extracts diffusion coefficients and anomalous exponents, classifies trajectories into diffusion models, and segments heterogeneous trajectories into diffusive states, through powerful, easy-to-use visualization tools. See more at https://github.com/gorkamunoz/andi-j .

title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates
summary: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous {beta}-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.

title: TRPP Ion Channels Function in the π-Conformation Rather Than the α-Conformation
summary: PKD2 (TRPP1) is a TRPP ion channel whose dysfunction causes autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Understanding its conformational states and gating mechanism is important for elucidating its function and for structure-based drug discovery. Cryo-EM structures of WT-PKD2 contain a local {pi}-helical turn in the S6 pore-lining helix ({pi}-conformation). In contrast, a fully -helical S6 (-conformation) was observed in the gain-of-function mutant F604P-PKD2 and interpreted as the open state, leading to the proposed {pi}-to- activation mechanism. However, whether the -conformation can support function has never been directly established. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the functional properties of the -and {pi}-conformations of PKD2. The -conformation remains dewetted unless the lower gate is widened beyond the conformational range observed in mammalian TRP channels. By contrast, the {pi}-conformation supports pore hydration and ion conduction following a small opening of the L677 gate, with simulated conductance comparable to experimental measurements. The closely related PKD2L1 (TRPP2) channel shows a similar dependence on conformation, with a hydrated {pi}-conformation and a dewetted -conformation. Together, these findings challenge the assignment of the -conformation as the conductive state and support a model in which the {pi}-conformation represents the functionally relevant state of TRPP channels. This model suggests that activation may involve an -to-{pi} transition rather than the previously proposed {pi}-to- transition, providing a new framework for understanding TRPP channel gating. This work sheds light on the molecular basis of polycystin channel dysfunction and could facilitate the development of PKD2-targeted therapeutic strategies for ADPKD.
